from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Two blocks collide on a frictionless floor.",
            "Block A moves toward Block B.",
            "Block B bounces off a wall.",
            "Block B strikes Block A again.",
            "We count total collisions until they separate."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Setup: The Two-Block Collision Puzzle", lecture_lines)
        
        # Define objects
        block_a = Square(side_length=0.8, color=WHITE, fill_opacity=1)
        label_a = Text("A", color=WHITE).next_to(block_a, UP)
        group_a = VGroup(block_a, label_a)
        
        block_b = Square(side_length=1.2, color=RED, fill_opacity=1)
        label_b = Text("B", color=WHITE).next_to(block_b, UP)
        group_b = VGroup(block_b, label_b)
        
        wall = Line(start=UP*2, end=DOWN*2, color=GREY).shift(RIGHT*4)
        
        self.place_at_grid(group_a, 'D2')
        self.place_at_grid(group_b, 'D4')
        self.add(wall)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(block_a.animate.set_color("#FFFF00"), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(group_a.animate.shift(RIGHT*1.5), run_time=1)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(block_b.animate.set_color("#00FFFF"), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(group_b.animate.shift(RIGHT*1), run_time=1)
        self.play(group_b.animate.shift(LEFT*0.5), run_time=0.5)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(group_b.animate.shift(LEFT*0.8), run_time=1)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        energy_label = Text("Energy: Conserved", color="#00FF00", font_size=20)
        self.place_at_grid(energy_label, 'A6')
        self.play(Write(energy_label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Geometry and physics produce Pi digits.", "Energy conservation creates circular constraints.", "Blocks act as a physical computer."]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion: Geometry meets Dynamics", lecture_lines)
        
        # Define visual elements
        circle = Circle(radius=1.5, color=BLUE)
        small_block = Square(side_length=0.4, color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=0.8)

        system = VGroup(small_block, big_block)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===

        self.place_at_grid(circle, 'C3', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(circle))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.place_in_area(system, 'C2', 'D4', scale_factor=0.8)
        # Indicate conservation (circle constraint)
        self.play(FadeIn(system))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        # Morphing the system to the circle concept
        self.play(
            system.animate.move_to(circle.get_center()),
            FadeOut(system),
            circle.animate.set_stroke(width=6, color=WHITE)
        )
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Pi Mystery: Counting Collisions to Calculate Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school students or curious science enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: The Two-Block Collision Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: two blocks of different masses (M1 and M2) on a frictionless floor. M1 moves toward M2, which is at rest near a wall. M1 hits M2, M2 hits the wall and bounces back, then M2 hits M1 again. We count every collision until M1 moves away forever.
sections.example: Visual: Two blocks. Block A is 1kg, Block B is 100kg. As they bounce, a counter on screen tracks: 1, 2, 3...

sections.title: Prerequisite: Elastic Collisions and Momentum
sections.content: Briefly explain the Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy. Use a 'Vector Arrow' animation to show how velocity changes direction during a collision, emphasizing that these are perfectly elastic (no energy lost).
sections.example: Animation: Two billiard balls hitting. The velocity vectors shrink and grow, demonstrating the math behind the 'rebound'.

sections.title: The Unexpected Pattern: Scaling Mass
sections.content: Reveal the core observation: If the mass ratio M2/M1 is a power of 100 (e.g., 1, 100, 10,000), the number of collisions is exactly the first few digits of Pi (3, 31, 314...).
sections.example: Table: M2/M1 = 1 -> 3 collisions; M2/M1 = 100 -> 31 collisions; M2/M1 = 10,000 -> 314 collisions.

sections.title: Visualizing the Physics: Phase Space Mapping
sections.content: Explain why this happens. By mapping the velocities of the two blocks as coordinates on a 2D plane (x, y), each collision is equivalent to a 'reflection' against a circular arc. The total number of collisions is equivalent to how many times a ray fits into a circular sector.
sections.example: Animation: A trajectory bouncing inside a circular wedge. The total angle of the wedge shrinks as the mass ratio increases, forcing the path to mimic the digits of Pi.

sections.title: Conclusion: Geometry meets Dynamics
sections.content: Summarize that Pi isn't just about circles on paper; it emerges naturally from any system where energy and momentum are conserved in a circular phase-space constraint. The blocks are essentially 'computing' Pi.
sections.example: Closing visual: The two blocks slowly morph into a spinning circle, tying the abstract digits of Pi back to the physical movement of the blocks.
